snapshot.title: SSC Quant: Simple & Compound Interest
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ SSC Quant Hook: SI: Same. CI: Effective rate x+y+xy/100. Diff 2yr: PR^2/100^2. Half yr: R/2, T*2. 3^x in T -> 3^y in (T/x)*y.

quick_notes.title: Simple Interest (SI)
quick_notes.detail: SI : (P × R × T) / 100. Interest remains same for every year.
quick_notes.explanation: Simple Interest (SI) is a method of calculating the extra money you pay or earn when you borrow or lend money, and it is always based only on the original amount. The original amount you borrow or lend is called the Principal (P), the percentage charged per year is the Rate of interest (R), and the number of years you keep the money is Time (T). To find the Simple Interest, you multiply the Principal by the Rate and by the Time, then divide by 100 using the formula SI = (P x R x T) / 100. Because the interest is never added to the Principal, the interest you pay or earn stays exactly the same every year for the entire Time period.

quick_notes.title: Compound Interest (CI)
quick_notes.detail: Amount : P(1 + R/100)^T. CI : Amount - Principal.
quick_notes.explanation: Compound interest is interest earned on both the original amount of money, called the Principal (P), and on any interest that has already been added. The total money you have after a certain number of years, called the Amount (A), is calculated using the formula A equals P times (1 plus R over 100) raised to the power T, where R is the yearly interest rate

quick_notes.title: CI vs SI Difference
quick_notes.detail: For 2 years: Diff : P(R/100)^2. For 3 years: Diff : [P(R/100)^2] × [(300 + R)/100]. (High Yield).
quick_notes.explanation: Compound interest (CI) is interest earned on both the original amount and any interest already earned, while simple interest (SI) is interest earned only on the original amount. P stands for the principal, the initial amount of money you start with. R stands for the rate of interest per year, written as a number like 10 for 10%. For two years, the difference between CI and SI is P times (R divided by 100) squared, written as P multiplied by (R/100) squared. For three years, the difference is that same result multiplied by (300 plus R) divided by 100.

quick_notes.title: Rate & Time (Installments)
quick_notes.detail: Quarterly: Rate/4, Time*4. Half-yearly: Rate/2, Time*2.
quick_notes.explanation: When you pay back a loan in installments, the interest rate and the time period must be adjusted to match how often you pay. For a quarterly payment plan, which means you pay every three months, you divide the annual interest rate by 4 to get the rate for each quarter, and you multiply the number of years by 4 to get the total number of quarterly payments. For a half-yearly payment plan, which means you pay every six months, you divide the annual interest rate by 2 to get the rate for each half-year, and you multiply the number of years by 2 to get the total number of half-yearly payments.

quick_notes.title: Successive Method for CI
quick_notes.detail: Use x + y + (xy/100) for effective rate. (e.g., 10% for 2 yrs : 21%. 5% for 2 yrs : 10.25%).
quick_notes.explanation: Compound interest (CI) is interest calculated on both the original amount and the interest already earned. When interest rates change each year, you can find the total percentage increase over two years using the formula x plus y plus (x times y divided by 100), where x is the first year's rate and y is the second year's rate. For example, if the rate is 10% for both years, the effective rate for the two years is 10 plus 10 plus (10 times 10 divided by 100) equals 21%, meaning the total growth is 21% of the original amount. Similarly, if the rate is 5% for both years, the effective rate is 5 plus 5 plus (5 times 5 divided by 100) equals 10.25%. This method works for any two successive rates, even if they are different.

lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Power of Compounding'. Simple Interest (SI) is constant every year, while Compound Interest (CI) is interest on interest.
